title: Log Analysis with awk and grep
markdown:
# Log Analysis with `awk` and `grep`

A production server generates thousands of log lines per minute. Raw logs contain everything — successful requests, errors, slow responses, and suspicious activity all mixed together. Reading them line by line is impossible. The job of a log analyst is to write targeted queries that reduce thousands of lines to the handful that actually matter.

In this lab, we use `grep` and `awk` — the two tools best suited for this job — to analyze a set of server access logs, extract patterns, identify bottlenecks, and produce a formatted weekly report.

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/878d7af2afc0c3d958cddbf61df06c985e664e46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2012/images/log-arch.svg)

By the end of this lab, you will be able to:

- Filter logs by status code, endpoint, and IP using `grep`
- Parse structured log records with `awk`
- Count, group, and rank log entries by field value
- Compute metrics like error rates and average response time
- Build a complete log analysis report using pipes and `tee`

## The Scenario: Weekly Log Review at `Poridhi.io`

The Poridhi.io API server has been running for a week. Every Monday, the ops team answers four questions before opening their backlog:

1. Which endpoints are getting the most traffic?
2. Which IPs are making the most requests?
3. How many errors occurred, and which endpoints are failing?
4. What is the average response time — and are any endpoints slow?

You have the week's access logs. Your job is to answer each question using `grep` and `awk`, then save the results as a report.

| What | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `loglab/access.log` | One week of server access logs |
| `grep` | Filter by status code, endpoint, or IP |
| `awk` | Count by field, rank by frequency, compute response time averages |
| `loglab/report.txt` | Final summary report saved with `tee` |

## Part 1: Understanding the Log Format

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/878d7af2afc0c3d958cddbf61df06c985e664e46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2012/images/log-example.svg)

Before querying data, understand its structure. Each line in the access log follows this format:

```
IP METHOD ENDPOINT STATUS RESPONSE_TIME
```

Example:

```
192.168.1.12 POST /api/upload 500 891ms
```

| Field | `awk` position | Meaning |
|-------|---------------|---------|
| IP address | `$1` | Client that sent the request |
| HTTP method | `$2` | GET, POST, DELETE, etc. |
| Endpoint | `$3` | The API path |
| Status code | `$4` | 200 = OK, 4xx = client error, 500 = server error |
| Response time | `$5` | Duration including `ms` suffix (e.g. `145ms`) |

Knowing the field positions lets you write `awk` rules without any guesswork.

## Part 3: Filtering Logs with `grep`

### Step 1: Filter by Status Code

Get all 500 server errors:

```bash
grep " 500 " loglab/access.log
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/878d7af2afc0c3d958cddbf61df06c985e664e46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2012/images/image-2.png)

The spaces around `500` prevent false matches against IP addresses or response times that might contain `500`.

Get all non-200 responses (errors and other codes):

```bash
grep -v " 200 " loglab/access.log
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/878d7af2afc0c3d958cddbf61df06c985e664e46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2012/images/image-3.png)

Here, `-v` inverts the match — returning lines that do NOT contain ` 200 `.

### Step 2: Filter by Endpoint or IP

Find all requests to `/api/upload`:

```bash
grep "/api/upload" loglab/access.log
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/878d7af2afc0c3d958cddbf61df06c985e664e46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2012/images/image-4.png)

Find all failed login attempts:

```bash
grep "/api/login" loglab/access.log | grep -v " 200 "
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/878d7af2afc0c3d958cddbf61df06c985e664e46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2012/images/image-5.png)

Piping two `grep` commands narrows the result in two passes — first by endpoint, then by status.

### Step 3: Count Error Events

```bash
# Total 500 errors
grep -c " 500 " loglab/access.log

# Total 4xx errors
grep -cE " 4[0-9]{2} " loglab/access.log
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/878d7af2afc0c3d958cddbf61df06c985e664e46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2012/images/image-6.png)

`-E` enables extended regex — `4[0-9]{2}` matches any three-digit code starting with 4.

**Why it matters**: `grep` quickly isolates the events you care about before handing the result to `awk`. On a 10-million-line log, filtering first makes a significant difference.

## Part 4: Analyzing Logs with `awk`

### Step 1: Count Requests per Endpoint

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/878d7af2afc0c3d958cddbf61df06c985e664e46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2012/images/awk-count.svg)

```bash
awk '{count[$3]++} END {for (ep in count) print count[ep], ep}' loglab/access.log | sort -rn
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/878d7af2afc0c3d958cddbf61df06c985e664e46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2012/images/image-7.png)

For each line, `count[$3]++` increments the counter for that endpoint. The `END` block runs after all lines are processed and prints every entry. `sort -rn` ranks from highest to lowest.

### Step 2: Find the Top Clients by Request Volume

```bash
awk '{count[$1]++} END {for (ip in count) print count[ip], ip}' loglab/access.log | sort -rn | head -5
```

Here, we count by IP address (`$1`) instead of endpoint. The top IPs might indicate heavy users or potential abuse. `head -5` limits the output to the top 5 clients.

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/878d7af2afc0c3d958cddbf61df06c985e664e46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2012/images/image-8.png)

An IP with unusually high traffic might indicate a scraper, a misconfigured retry loop, or a legitimate heavy user that needs rate-limiting.

### Step 3: Count Errors per Endpoint

Which endpoints are producing 500 errors?

```bash
awk '$4 == 500 {count[$3]++} END {for (ep in count) print count[ep], ep}' loglab/access.log | sort -rn
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/878d7af2afc0c3d958cddbf61df06c985e664e46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2012/images/image-9.png)

Here, `$4 == 500` is a row filter — only lines where the status field equals 500 are counted. This quickly identifies which endpoints are failing most often.

### Step 4: Calculate Average Response Time per Endpoint

Response times are stored as `891ms` — strip the `ms` suffix using `gsub` before doing arithmetic:

```bash
awk '{gsub(/ms/, "", $5); sum[$3] += $5; count[$3]++} END {for (ep in sum) printf "%.1fms  %s\n", sum[ep]/count[ep], ep}' \
  loglab/access.log | sort -rn
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/878d7af2afc0c3d958cddbf61df06c985e664e46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2012/images/image-10.png)

`gsub(/ms/, "", $5)` removes `ms` from field 5 in-place, converting `891ms` to `891` so arithmetic works. `sum[$3] += $5` accumulates total response time per endpoint, while `count[$3]++` counts requests. The `END` block computes and prints the average response time for each endpoint.

**Why it matters**: `awk` turns a raw log into a statistical summary in a single pass. The same technique works on any structured log — nginx, Apache, application logs — as long as you know the field positions.

## Part 5: Building the Weekly Report

Combine everything into one report that answers all four questions from the scenario. Use `tee` to display and save simultaneously:

```bash
{
  echo "=== Weekly Access Log Report ==="

  echo ""
  echo "--- Total Requests ---"
  wc -l < loglab/access.log

  echo ""
  echo "--- Top 5 Endpoints by Traffic ---"
  awk '{count[$3]++} END {for (ep in count) print count[ep], ep}' loglab/access.log | sort -rn | head -5

  echo ""
  echo "--- Top 5 Clients by Request Volume ---"
  awk '{count[$1]++} END {for (ip in count) print count[ip], ip}' loglab/access.log | sort -rn | head -5

  echo ""
  echo "--- Error Count by Status Code ---"
  awk '$4 != 200 {count[$4]++} END {for (code in count) print count[code], code}' loglab/access.log | sort -rn

  echo ""
  echo "--- Average Response Time by Endpoint ---"
  awk '{gsub(/ms/, "", $5); sum[$3] += $5; count[$3]++} END {for (ep in sum) printf "%.1fms  %s\n", sum[ep]/count[ep], ep}' \
    loglab/access.log | sort -rn

} | tee loglab/report.txt
```

Verify the report was saved:

```bash
cat loglab/report.txt
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/878d7af2afc0c3d958cddbf61df06c985e664e46/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2012/images/image-11.png)

**Why it matters**: A single command block that generates a formatted, saved report is more useful than running individual queries and reading output manually. Once built, this becomes a script you run every Monday morning — or a cron job that runs automatically.

## Conclusion

In this lab, we turned raw access logs into a structured weekly report using only two tools:

- `grep` filtered the log down to specific status codes, endpoints, and IPs
- `awk` parsed the structured fields, counted occurrences, and computed response time averages
- Combining them with pipes and `tee` produced a single, reusable reporting command

Real log analysis at scale follows exactly this pattern — filter first with `grep` to reduce volume, then process the filtered output with `awk` to extract meaning. The commands you built here translate directly to nginx logs, Apache logs, or any other line-structured log format.
